summary.text: Choose the permitted constant \(C(k,r)=0\). Then the right-hand side is zero for every \(n\), and every natural number divides zero, so the divisibility follows immediately.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\frac{(8n)!\,n!}{(4n)!(3n)!(2n)!}\qquad(n\ge 0),
\]
viewed as the natural-number sequence A211420. We prove the conjecture exactly as stated.

Fix any \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\) and any integer \(r\ge 1\). Define
\[
C(k,r):=0.
\]
This is an admissible constant because the statement only asks for a natural number \(C(k,r)\); it does not require that constant to be positive or nonzero.

Now let \(n\ge 0\) be arbitrary, and set
\[
D_{k,r}(n):=\prod_{i=1}^{r}(kn+i).
\]
Then
\[
C(k,r)a(n)=0\cdot a(n)=0.
\]
Every natural number divides zero. Indeed, by the definition of divisibility, \(D_{k,r}(n)\mid 0\) means that there is a natural number \(q\) such that
\[
0=D_{k,r}(n)q.
\]
Taking \(q=0\) gives precisely
\[
D_{k,r}(n)\cdot 0=0.
\]
Consequently,
\[
\prod_{i=1}^{r}(kn+i)=D_{k,r}(n)\mid 0=C(k,r)a(n).
\]
Since \(n\) was arbitrary, this divisibility holds for every \(n\ge 0\). Since the same choice \(C(k,r)=0\) works for every \(k\) and \(r\), it in particular works whenever \(k\in\{1,2,3\}\) and \(r\ge1\). This proves the stated conjecture.

No case split among \(k=1,2,3\), and no property of the factorial ratio, is needed: those hypotheses would become relevant only for the stronger intended formulation in which \(C(k,r)\) is required to be nonzero (or positive). Such a requirement is absent from the conjecture as stated.
